summary: This informational memo covers what application developers should consider when moving to IPv6. It describes scenarios and aspects of application transition and gives guidelines for writing programs that work with IPv6, IPv4, or both.

plainLanguage.summary: When a town changes address styles, programs that use addresses need updating too. This document gives programmers advice on making their programs work with both old and new addresses.

subtitle: How network applications should be adapted so they work over IPv6, IPv4 or both during the transition.

tldr.problem: Network transition mechanisms say nothing about whether applications support IPv6, so programs written for IPv4 can fail or confuse users as IPv6 is deployed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts application transition into four cases and recommends porting to IP version-independent applications that ask the resolver for all addresses and try each until one works.
tldr.outcome: Applications supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 are the most advisable case, since one program then works with any mix of nodes and no one has to pick between program versions.

today: RFC 4038 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its guidance rests on the socket APIs of RFC 3493 and RFC 3542.

sections.title: Four Cases of Application Transition
sections.content:
Basic IPv6 transition mechanisms such as dual-stack deployment and tunneling take no stance on whether applications support IPv6. This RFC covers two topics: how network transition techniques affect applications, and how to build IPv6-capable or protocol-independent applications using the standard socket APIs. It focuses on applications written against low-level APIs, such as C programs using standard libraries.

It sorts the situations into four cases, after the case where nothing supports IPv6.

  • Case 1: IPv4-only applications on a dual-stack node.
  • Case 2: separate IPv4-only and IPv6-only applications on a dual-stack node, such as ping and ping6.
  • Case 3: applications supporting both versions on a dual-stack node.
  • Case 4: applications supporting both versions on an IPv4-only node.

The first two cases are not interesting in the longer term, because few applications are inherently tied to one IP version.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can know only the old addresses, only the new ones, or both. It might also run on a computer that only understands the old ones.

sections.title: Why Application Transition Is Hard
sections.content:
Support for IPv6 in the operating system and in applications are unrelated, so the two will coexist in various combinations for a long time. A both-versions application may have to work in an IPv4-only node, whether IPv6 is disabled or just not connected.

The DNS does not say which IP version a peer application speaks. If a server application has no IPv6 support but runs on a dual-stack machine that has an AAAA record for other services, a client that tries the IPv6 address will fail to connect. SRV records would avoid this but were not used widely enough. The RFC says applications should request all addresses without address family constraints and try the records in some order until one works.

Keeping many versions of one program is also painful, because users struggle to choose the right one. A "wrapper application" that picks the version is judged not robust, so hybrid applications supporting both are preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone book entry does not tell you which kind of phone the other person has. So you try the numbers one by one until someone picks up.

sections.title: How Each Scenario Behaves
sections.content:
IPv4 applications on a dual-stack node. The first priority is to port them. If source code is unavailable, Bump-in-the-Stack or Bump-in-the-API can help, but the RFC strongly recommends not using them when source is available, and they do not work with applications such as FTP that exchange IP addresses as data.

IPv6 applications on a dual-stack node. A simple one-to-one port yields an IPv6-only program. On most dual-stack systems such a program can still talk to IPv4 peers through IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, where ::FFFF:x.y.z.w stands for IPv4 address x.y.z.w. Setting the IPV6_V6ONLY socket option turns this off. Shipping two versions (like telnet and telnet6) is not recommended.

IPv4/IPv6 applications on a dual-stack node. This is the most advisable case. Implementations typically prefer IPv6 and, if it fails, version-independent applications go on to try IPv4 addresses from the resolver's list.

IPv4/IPv6 applications on an IPv4-only node. Such programs must cope when IPv6 is disabled or missing. A loop that tries AF_INET6 and then AF_INET must not quit when the first socket() call fails with EPROTONOSUPPORT or EAFNOSUPPORT.
sections.plainLanguage: Best is one program that speaks both address styles and tries the new one first. If that does not work, it quietly tries the old one.

sections.title: Porting Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists the common IP version dependencies in applications: address presentation format, the transport API, name and address resolution, specific IP dependencies, and multicast.

  • Presentation. Buffers for IPv4 address strings may be too small for IPv6, so fix overflows. Because colons already structure IPv6 addresses, an address with a port needs brackets, as in http://[2001:db8::1]:80. Literal addresses are strongly discouraged as general input; use host names and DNS.
  • APIs. Use structures able to hold 128-bit addresses and generic address structures. IPv6 has no broadcast addresses, so applications can use multicast instead.
  • Resolution. The new functions are getaddrinfo() and getnameinfo(). It is recommended to obtain all configured addresses.
  • Address selection. Source address selection is usually left to the node, following RFC 3484. For destinations, try each address in the list until communication succeeds.
  • Framing. UDP-based applications can stay within the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1280 bytes, force fragmentation, or find the optimal size. The RFC takes no stance on which is best.
  • Storing addresses. Prefer names to addresses, since addresses can change after renumbering and one node may be reached by several.
  • Multicast. IPv6 multicast addresses encode scope, and IPv4 multicast addresses have no direct equivalents for all cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Old programs assumed addresses are short and written with dots. New addresses are longer and use colons, so programs need bigger boxes and need to ask names, not numbers, wherever they can.

sections.title: Writing Version-Independent Applications
sections.content:
The RFC recommends dual applications that avoid IP dependencies, ideally hiding any that remain behind a communication library. All structures and APIs should be IP version-independent: avoid struct in_addr, in6_addr, sockaddr_in and sockaddr_in6, and use struct sockaddr_storage instead, so no extra address-family parameter is needed.

Where getaddrinfo() returns several addresses, client code should try all of them until connection succeeds. If socket(), connect(), bind() or another call fails, the code should go on to the next address, including when the address family is not supported. The RFC gives example TCP server and client programs built this way.

Applications must not be required to tell apart normal addresses from NAT-PT translated addresses, or other special addresses including IPv4-mapped ones. If that distinction is needed, it belongs in the kernel or system libraries.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the program so it does not care which address style it gets. Hand it a list and let it try each entry until one works.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
General IPv6 transition security is outside the scope of the memo. It does point out that cycling through addresses until a working one is found helps availability and robustness when moving to IPv6, and doing this properly is critical to avoid loss of service.

IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses cut both ways. They ease application transition but make it hard to ensure their use was legitimate. Some systems disable them by default, which is a legitimate concern, but doing so breaks the transition path for server applications that bind to a single wildcard socket and forces developers to rewrite them.
sections.plainLanguage: Trying every address until one works keeps the service from going dark. The shortcut that lets old and new addresses mix is handy but harder to keep an eye on.
